Attack on Pearl Harbor. On December seventh, nineteen forty-one, the Japanese Imperial Navy launched a surprise attack on the United States naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. The assault sank eight battleships and killed over eleven hundred sailors, shocking the American public and leading to the U.S. declaration of war against Japan the next day, formally drawing the nation into World War II.

The attack was carried out by three hundred fifty-three Japanese aircraft from six aircraft carriers, led by Commander Mitsuo Fuchida and coordinated from a depth of roughly two hundred seventy-five kilometers northeast of the island. The Japanese forces destroyed or damaged eight battleships, three cruisers, and one hundred eighty-eight aircraft, with total casualties exceeding twelve hundred American military personnel.

President Franklin D. Roosevelt called it "a date which will live in infamy" in his address to Congress on December eighth, nineteen forty-one. The attack aimed to neutralize the U.S. Pacific Fleet and buy Japan time to consolidate control over Southeast Asia and the Pacific. Japanese planners achieved tactical surprise by treating Pearl Harbor as the main target, and the Americans received no warning despite some radio intercepts. Fortunately, the U.S. aircraft carrier fleet was at sea during the attack, preserving the most valuable warships and enabling American recovery.

The assault unified American political will for war. Even isolationist politicians voted for the declaration, shifting the nation's entire strategic posture. Pearl Harbor served as the precipitating cause that brought the United States into the broader conflict and set the stage for the battles of Midway and the Coral Sea that would follow.
